theme: Woes; visions; the booth of David rebuilt
readingInstruction: Read Amos 6:1-9:15. The book ends with woes against the complacent, five visions of judgment, a confrontation with the priest of Bethel, and a final promise of restoration. Read the closing verses slowly.
settingTheScene: The last chapters of Amos strip away the last illusions. The wealthy are comfortable and indifferent. Visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line, and a basket of summer fruit show that the end is near. Then, in the last paragraph, the tone changes completely. God promises to rebuild David’s fallen shelter and to restore his people. It is among the great hopeful notes in the prophets.
observation: “Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria” (6:1).
“Who lie on beds of ivory and stretch themselves out on their couches… but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (6:4-6).
Amos sees a plumb line: “Behold, I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them” (7:7-8).

Amaziah the priest tells Amos to go home. Amos says, “I was no prophet, nor a prophet’s son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs. But the LORD took me from following the flock” (7:14-15).
A basket of summer fruit: “The end has come upon my people Israel” (8:1-2).
“Hear this, you who trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end” (8:4).
“Behold, the days are coming… when I will send a famine on the land… of hearing the words of the LORD” (8:11).
“In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old” (9:11).
interpretation:
The woes of chapter 6 describe a comfortable elite: lying on ivory couches, eating lambs from the flock, singing idle songs, drinking wine by the bowl, and anointing themselves with the best oils. “But they are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph.” The problem is not wealth itself but indifference. They are at ease while the nation is falling apart. Complacency is a sin when others suffer.

The visions show God’s patience and its limit. In the first two visions, Amos pleads, and God relents. In the third, a plumb line, there is no more relenting. The plumb line measures a wall. The wall is crooked, and it will be torn down. The standard is God’s own righteousness, and Israel does not match it.

Amaziah, the priest, tries to silence Amos: “Never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary.” The priest’s complaint is revealing. The place of worship has become the king’s property. Amos answers by telling his story. He was a farmer. God took him. He has no choice but to speak. A person called by God cannot be silenced by human authority.

Chapter 8 describes a famine unlike any other, not of bread or water but of hearing the words of the LORD. When God’s word is rejected long enough, it is withdrawn. It is one of the most frightening judgments in the Bible. Yet it also shows how precious the word of God is.

But the book does not end in judgment. The last words are promises: God will raise up the fallen booth of David, restore the fortunes of his people, and plant them in their land, “never again to be uprooted.” The same God who judges also restores. The nations are included: “that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name.” The hope reaches beyond Israel.
connection: In Acts 15:15-18, James quotes Amos 9:11-12 to show that the inclusion of the Gentiles in the church fulfills God’s promise to rebuild David’s tent. Jesus is the son of David who rebuilds the ruins. Jesus said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). John 12:48 and Hebrews 2:3 warn about neglecting God’s word. Luke 16:19-31, the rich man and Lazarus, is a New Testament echo of Amos 6.
application:
Ask if you are at ease while others suffer. What would it look like to be grieved over the ruin of Joseph?

Treasure God’s word, and use it, knowing that there can be a famine of hearing it.

Thank God for the promise to rebuild David’s fallen tent, fulfilled in Christ.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have grown complacent.
Ask him to grieve you over what grieves him.
Ask him to measure you by his plumb line and make you straight.
